blindSummary:
A 2025 anti-vilification law (passed April 2025) created both civil and criminal vilification offences and extended protection beyond race and religion to disability, gender identity, sex, sex characteristics, sexual orientation and personal association (new civil grounds added to this state/province's equality law). This state/province is the only jurisdiction in the country where public incitement against a trans person is now a criminal charge, not merely a civil complaint. A 2006 human-rights charter binds public authorities and provides an independent review mechanism that some other states/provinces lack.

A coronial inquest into the deaths of five young transgender women found the local police force failed the search for one of them. The coroner issued nine recommendations calling for an overhaul of missing-persons risk assessment for trans people. Advocates characterised the police handling as a serious failure of justice. The finding documents an institutional failure, but the reform process and the 2025 legislation represent a corrective institutional response.

Academic review confirms that this state/province's LGBT prison protections are policy-based and not legally enforceable, a cross-jurisdictional weakness.

The criminal vilification offence is the strongest new legal protection in the country and the charter adds a structural review mechanism, but the coronial finding on police failure toward a specifically vulnerable sub-population (trans women in sex-work-adjacent contexts) and the thinness of prison policy limit the positive signal.

This state/province's equal-opportunity and human-rights commission fact sheet explaining the new anti-hate laws: the 2025 law passed in April 2025 creates civil vilification grounds in the equality law (inciting hatred; hateful conduct a reasonable member of the target group would consider hateful) and criminal offences in the criminal code; protection extends to disability, gender identity, race, religious belief, sex, sex characteristics and sexual orientation (plus association), with civil grounds commencing 15 April 2026.

National-broadcaster report (29 August 2024) on a coronial inquest into the deaths of five young transgender women in the state's largest city during the pandemic (lead case: reported missing December 2020, died by suicide aged 28): the coroner identified multiple local police failings and made nine recommendations, including urgent investment in trans health care and reform of missing-persons practice; the government is reviewing the recommendations.

A national newspaper report (29 August 2024, paywalled - partial text retrieved) from the coroners court inquest: the coroner urged an overhaul of missing-persons procedures after the probe into the deaths of young trans women, companion coverage to the broadcaster account of the nine recommendations.
